entries.definition: A GSAT variant that breaks ties among best-scoring variable flips by choosing the variable flipped least recently in the current attempt, using a fixed arbitrary order for ties among never-flipped variables.

claims.statement: Start an attempt with a random complete assignment as in GSAT and initialize the attempt-local flip history. If the formula is not satisfied, evaluate each variable by the change in the total number of satisfied clauses caused by flipping it. Form the set of variables with greatest score increase, including zero or negative best gains when no improving flip exists. Among those candidates, choose the one whose last flip in the current attempt was longest ago. Variables never flipped in that attempt are treated as oldest; when several such variables are candidates, use an arbitrary fixed ordering. Flip the chosen variable, update its timestamp and continue within the declared attempt budget. New attempts reset the current-attempt history. The source retains the GenSAT outer attempts and GSAT candidate-score rule while changing the picking rule.

entries.name: Novelty SAT heuristic
entries.definition: A clause-based SAT local-search heuristic that ranks candidate flips by total violation count with oldest-variable tie breaks, normally selects the best candidate, and sometimes selects the second-best when the best was the most recently flipped variable in that clause.
entries.identity_notes: This is the Novelty SAT heuristic introduced by McAllester, Selman and Kautz in 1997, not the general idea of novelty or novelty-search objectives in evolutionary computation. It ranks only variables of a selected unsatisfied clause by the global post-flip objective. Its age-conditional choice differs from HSAT’s global best-score tie selection, WalkSAT/SKC’s break-only score and freebie priority, and tabu inadmissibility. Novelty+ adds a separate random-walk branch and is not an exact alias. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 52 and 53 lines respectively. All twenty unique hit contents were inspected: neighboring variant references, saved reviews and discovery leads, generic novelty wording and an ignored Sphinx comment, not existing candidate records. The checkout differences are retained in the ledger. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five full native neighboring records were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Hoos’s 1999 Theorem 3 shows that Novelty without random restart is essentially incomplete for every noise setting: there are satisfiable inputs and reachable search states from which a model is never found. This statement is about the unrestarted heuristic, not every solver that wraps it in an unbounded random-restart scheme.

A verified model is a sound positive result, but exhausting a finite budget is not an UNSAT certificate. The 1997 empirical noise-level and optimality invariants are not general convergence theorems or guaranteed optimal tuning rules.

The two-candidate rule needs an explicit convention for unit clauses and for initial/tied timestamps among never-flipped variables. Empty clauses require separate handling. The short source description does not certify an executable choice for every such boundary.

A nonrecent best candidate is selected even when p=1; a score tie is first resolved by age. No SKC zero-break priority, tabu prohibition or R-Novelty score-gap formula is silently inserted. Weighted MAX-SAT extensions and later Novelty variants need separate scope.

claims.statement: Begin from a complete assignment and, while it is unsatisfying, randomly choose an unsatisfied clause. Rank its candidate variables by the total number of unsatisfied clauses that would remain after each flip, preferring a less recently flipped variable when objective scores tie. Let the first two candidates be best and second-best. If the best is not the most recently flipped variable anywhere in the selected clause, choose it. Otherwise choose the second-best with probability p and the best with probability 1−p, for p in [0,1]. Flip the chosen variable, update its timestamp and repeat under the chosen outer search and stopping policy. The score uses the global net effect of a flip, not breakcount alone. The noise coin is conditional on recency; it is not an unconditional random selection from all clause variables.

entries.name: R-Novelty SAT heuristic
entries.definition: A Novelty-derived SAT heuristic whose choice between the best and second-best flips depends on their objective-score gap when the best variable was most recently flipped; its original 1997 search strategy also includes a periodic random clause-variable move.
entries.identity_notes: This record follows the full 1997 R-Novelty parameterization and its stated every-100-flip random override, retaining the distinction from the core score-gap selector and from the 1999 R-Novelty+ extension. The 2004 solver description instead labels a periodic-override configuration Rnovelty+ and describes only the p=0.5 selector case. Those differing source conventions are not treated as exact synonyms or interchangeable completeness guarantees. The checkout differences are retained in the ledger. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five full native neighboring records were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Hoos1999 Theorem 4 and its continuation show that the unrestarted R-Novelty strategy is essentially incomplete for arbitrary noise settings even with its every-100-step override. A periodic random move can occur at phases that never expose a needed variable; its mere presence does not establish asymptotic success.

The 1999 R-Novelty+ method removes the periodic override and adds a positive random-walk probability at each step. Its guarantee relies on possible arbitrarily long random-walk sequences, not a deterministic schedule. The 2004 source uses the plus name differently and its cycling-prevention statement is not adopted as a guarantee.

The d>=1 branch formulation uses age-based score tie breaking. Initial timestamp ties, unit clauses with no second candidate, empty clauses and exact counter/reset conventions need explicit implementation decisions; a d=0 probability rule is not invented here.

Parameters p and the periodic schedule have different roles. Score gaps are in unweighted clause counts; changing them to weighted or real-valued objectives requires a new specification. Finite failure is not an UNSAT proof, and no author solver or benchmark was executed.

claims.statement: Use Novelty’s randomly selected unsatisfied clause, post-flip total-violation ranking and oldest-variable tie break. If the best candidate is not the most recently flipped variable in that clause, select it. Otherwise let d be the second-best post-flip violation count minus the best count; the 1997 rule assumes d>=1. If p<0.5 and d>1, choose the best. If p<0.5 and d=1, choose the second-best with probability 2p and otherwise the best. If p>=0.5 and d=1, choose the second-best. If p>=0.5 and d>1, choose the second-best with probability 2(p−0.5) and otherwise the best. Independently of this ordinary selection rule, the 1997 strategy specifies that every 100 flips it chooses a random variable from the selected clause instead. Update the chosen variable’s flip timestamp. At p=0.5 the recency-triggered rule picks second-best for gap one and best for a larger gap; that special case is not the full parameterized method.

claims.statement: Maintain a complete truth assignment and stop successfully when all clauses are satisfied. Otherwise randomly choose an unsatisfied nonempty clause. If any candidate has breakcount zero, choose one such candidate at random. Only when there is no zero-break candidate, choose a random variable from the selected clause with probability p; with probability 1−p choose a candidate of minimum breakcount, breaking ties randomly. Flip the chosen variable and repeat under the application’s stopping budget. The noise parameter, CNF encoding, initialization and outer budgets affect behavior. No single best p, universal speedup or numerical benchmark claim is curated. Empty clauses or empty candidate sets require explicit handling outside the described nonempty-variable flip rule.

The record curates the move policy and its stated GSAT context, not an executed solver or a certification of every loop boundary. The original GSAT pre-flip-only pseudocode boundary remains an implementation choice to declare.

claims.statement: Maintain a complete assignment of the variables in the input CNF formula. Stop successfully when it satisfies the formula. Otherwise, with fixed probability p, select uniformly from the distinct variables appearing in at least one currently unsatisfied clause and flip the chosen variable. With probability 1−p, evaluate all single-variable flips and choose a largest increase in the total number of satisfied clauses, breaking tied best choices randomly as in GSAT. The random and greedy branches can make non-improving moves. The extension can use the GSAT outer random-initialization, per-attempt flip budget and restart/attempt budget. The 1994 paper explicitly explains the duplicate-free variable list, which gives equal probabilities to eligible variables even when their clause occurrence counts differ.
